title: Even his back ached
hookLine: the old Buddha warms his back in the sun; Ananda sees his skin loosen
tomorrow: A friend gives the hard thing

lines: AN OLD MAN IN THE SUN.
cards: Evening in Savatthi, at the Eastern Park, in the mansion of Migara's mother. The Buddha has come out of his afternoon seclusion. He's an old man now, sitting in the western sun, warming his back.
Ananda, his attendant, comes over and begins to rub his limbs with his hands.
It's the kind of moment people who care for an aging parent describe: hands on their arms, and suddenly the skin seems thinner than you remembered. Ananda notices, and he says it out loud.

teach.b: It's wonderful, sir, it's amazing. Your complexion is no longer clear and bright. Your limbs are slack and wrinkled.
Your body is bent forward. And there's a change in your senses: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body. It's a blunt thing to say to your teacher, and the Buddha doesn't flinch.
So it is, Ananda, he says. In youth one is subject to aging; in health, to sickness; in life, to death.
Then he speaks a verse that turns on aging itself, scolding it: shame on you, wretched old age, maker of ugliness.
Even someone who lives a hundred years, he says, is bound for death; aging spares no one, it crushes everything.
And then, the text says, he gets up and goes into town for alms. That last detail is the whole teaching: he names it, scolds it in verse, and goes on with the day.
Elsewhere in the canon there are other glimpses, like a day when his back hurts and he asks Sariputta to teach in his place while he lies down to rest it. The texts don't hide the Buddha's body.
They show it aging, aching, ordinary. Some readers find that a comfort. Awakening, in this telling, didn't exempt even him from an old man's back.

how: Buddhist teachers often tell this scene when teaching on aging and impermanence, and in Buddhist communities caring for elders, including elderly monks and nuns, is counted as a meritorious act.

o: old age, which spares no one
a long life as a reward for virtue
the wisdom that comes with age

games.q: even his back ached: tap the pairs.
p: where the Buddha warmed his back
taught when the Buddha's back hurt

s: the texts say the Buddha's body never aged
Ananda sees his loose skin, bent posture and changing senses.
after the verse on old age, the Buddha goes for alms
he names it, then goes on with the day.
Ananda's remark made the Buddha angry
he answers simply: so it is.

games.q: you're Ananda. rubbing your teacher's arms, you see how old his body has become. what do you do?
o: say nothing; it would be disrespectful.
say it out loud: how changed you are.
games.why: Ananda says it plainly, and the Buddha agrees: so it is. aging spares no one. then he gets up and goes for alms.

practice: If you can, turn your back toward a window or a warm lamp, rest your hands on your forearms, and feel the skin, the warmth, the years in it.
Then bring to mind someone older whom you love, and picture warming their back, rubbing their arms, without hurry. Notice what tenderness feels like.

wordCard.voice: jara. The Pali and Sanskrit word for old age, spoken by the aging Buddha to Ananda in the evening sun: so it is; even life in the body ends in this. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit jara: old age, aging; SN 48.41 is named the Jara Sutta for it.

carryVoice: Your line: even his. Aging gets named, and the day still goes on, gently. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 33 (Sangiti Sutta), the aching back
